title: Homunculus and Dermatome Map
description: Interactive two-panel map. Learners click a body region on a front-view body outline and see where it is represented on the opposite primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), drawn as a homunculus-style strip, along with the spinal dermatome level (ISNCSCI key point) or cranial nerve that carries it. Includes a quiz mode with feedback.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
learningObjectives: Locate where a touched body region is represented on the opposite primary somatosensory cortex.
Name the spinal level (dermatome) or cranial nerve that carries touch from that region.
Explain why body parts with dense receptors, such as the lips and thumb, occupy larger areas of the somatosensory map.
prerequisites: Lobes of the cerebral cortex and the central sulcus (Chapter 4)
Sensory pathways cross to the opposite side of the brain
Basic structure of the spinal cord and spinal nerves (Chapter 1)
keyQuestions: Why does touch on the right hand activate the left hemisphere?
Why do the lips and hands get so much more cortex than the trunk?
Which spinal levels carry touch from the thumb, middle finger, and little finger?
Why does the face have no spinal dermatome?
misconceptions: The size of a body part's area on the somatosensory map matches the body part's physical size.
Touch from one side of the body is processed on the same side of the brain.
Dermatome borders are identical in every person and every textbook.
The face is supplied by cervical spinal nerves.
dataSources: Dermatome key points: ISNCSCI key sensory points as listed in Wikipedia, Dermatome (anatomy), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dermatome_(anatomy)
Homunculus order: OpenStax Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience 9.2, https://openstax.org/books/introduction-behavioral-neuroscience/pages/9-2-somatosensation-in-the-central-nervous-system
Cortex segment sizes are illustrative, not measured.
